chapter 01 · transformer — part 1 of 5

From tokens to vectors

Attention is handed a sequence of vectors. This is where those vectors come from — tokenizer, embedding matrix, word2vec — and what a sentence does to a dictionary entry once it has one.

Where this sits: a decoder-only transformer

Before the mechanism, the map — because attention on its own predicts nothing. It is one sub-layer, inside a block, that repeats.

So what does that sub-layer actually do? It takes n vectors and returns n vectors, where each output is a blend of the inputs — and each position chooses its own blend. Nothing is created and nothing is removed; information is moved.

The effect on a single token's vector is the thing to hold on to:

before attention   this token, alone
after  attention   this token, in this context
Worked on one sentence, and what repeating it buys

“The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired.” At the it position, it's query matches animal's key more strongly than street's, so the output at that position comes back carrying animal's value. The pronoun has been resolved — not by a grammar rule, but by a weighted read the model learned to perform. The MLP that follows then works on a vector that already knows what it refers to.

And because the block repeats, this compounds: an early layer may settle local syntax, a middle one a long-range reference, a later one the gist of the whole passage. Each pass lets every token see one hop further, through whatever the previous pass already gathered — which is exactly the two-layer composition p1 catches in the act.

The model below is the decoder-only stack: GPT-style, and what essentially every current LLM is. Worth naming, because it is not the architecture in the 2017 paper:

shapeused forattention in it
decoder-only
GPT, Llama — the diagram below		generation: predict the next token, foreverself-attention, causally masked so position i cannot see past itself
encoder-only
BERT and relatives		understanding a whole input at once — classification, embeddingsself-attention, unmasked — every token sees every token
encoder–decoder
the original 2017 transformer		translation: one sequence in, a different one outall three — masked self-attention in the decoder, unmasked in the encoder, plus cross-attention between them

The mechanism on this page is identical in all three. What changes is only the wiring around it: whether a mask is applied, and whether keys and values come from the same sequence as the queries (self-attention) or a different one (cross-attention). Part 2 builds the encoder–decoder version and covers cross-attention; this page stays with the decoder-only case, because it is the one the rest of the course needs.

At training time, both sides are inputs. The diagram reads like a pipeline, but a translation model is trained by feeding the Chinese and its English counterpart in at once — left column and right column simultaneously. What comes out of the top is not a translation, it is a loss, and backpropagation walks it back into every parameter. The sequential, one-token- at-a-time behaviour you see from a deployed model is an inference behaviour; it is not how the thing was trained. (Why that gap matters: parallel to train, sequential to generate.)

Two stages, in the author's framing — and the whole of this page is the second one:

Three things follow, and they are what makes the rest of the page make sense:

  • Attention's output is not a prediction. It is an edit added to a running vector. The prediction happens once, at the very end, from the last position's final vector.
  • Shape in = shape out. n × d_model both ways. Attention mixes across positions without changing the container — which is precisely why you can run 100 of them in a row.
  • Each block does one of each. Attention is the only step where a token can see another token; the MLP then processes every position alone. Mix, think, mix, think, N times.

So when the rest of this page says "the output b¹", that vector is not an answer — it is what gets added to position 1's running total before the next block sees it. The full path, tokenizer to sampled token, is part 2.

The problem attention is solving

Before the mechanism, the goal. Given a sequence of vectors a¹…aⁿ, each output bi must be built from whichever other positions actually matter for position i — and which ones matter differs for every token, every sentence, and every layer. It can't be fixed in advance, so it has to be computed from the content itself:

What exactly are a¹…aⁿ? Vectors — already embedded. Attention never sees characters, words, or token IDs. Before it runs, the text has been tokenized to integer IDs and each ID has looked up a learned vector of width d_model.

But which vectors depends on where in the stack you are, and this is the part worth pinning down:

layeraⁱ is…
the first blockthe token embedding, plus position — “this word, somewhere in the sentence”
every later blockthe residual stream at that point: that position's running vector, already edited by every block before it

So in block 1, a³ means roughly “the token 'street'.” By block 20 the vector at position 3 may encode “the thing the pronoun later refers to, in a sentence about an animal being tired” — same slot, same shape, accumulated meaning. Attention does not know or care which; it takes n vectors and returns n vectors, which is exactly what lets the identical layer run at the bottom of the stack and at the top.

Before attention: how a word becomes a vector

That note says aⁱ arrives already embedded. Here is the step it skips — and it is worth seeing, because the usual phrase “embedding lookup” hides what is actually happening.

That orthogonality is the problem the embedding solves. A one-hot vector of length M (the vocabulary) is multiplied by an M × N matrix, and out comes a vector of length N — much smaller, and no longer orthogonal to its neighbours:

Why that reframing is worth the trouble. “Lookup table” suggests a filing cabinet — a vector stored per word, nothing more. “Change of basis” says what the table is for: the new axes need not be orthogonal, so the new coordinates can place related words near one another. The geometry is the point. It is also the cleanest way to see why the embedding for a Hi-C patch is the same operation — no one-hot to select a row, so the matrix acts on the whole input instead of picking from it.

The new basis need not be orthogonal — which is what lets it encode anything

Where the embedding matrix comes from: word2vec

Choosing those axes is itself a training problem. Here is the obvious way to pose it — and it fails, which is the instructive part.

The reason is the geometry from two figures ago. One-hot vectors are mutually orthogonal and equidistant, so the only fact present in the data is identity — and reconstruction asks for exactly that fact back. There is no shared structure for the bottleneck to exploit, so it settles on an arbitrary reversible code. Compression only buys meaning when the things being compressed have something in common; isolated tokens have nothing.

word2vec's move is to change the target. Stop asking the network to reproduce the token. Ask it to predict the token's company — which is a fact about the corpus that identity alone cannot answer. Two directions, same idea:

Look at the little vector diagrams under each. CBOW draws the target as the resultant of its context vectors — which is the mechanism behind your dictionary analogy, made literal:

word2vec 更像是编词典. A dictionary explains a target word using other words. word2vec's latent space does the same thing with addition — 用其它的词向量去合成目标词向量. That is what the blue + in CBOW is.

The task is a pretext; the geometry is the product. Take 这是一个 ___ 苹果. The blank accepts 红, 绿, 便宜 — all reasonable, so the model cannot be right. That is not a defect. The window is deliberately small, and the goal was never cloze accuracy: it is that after training, 红 · 绿 · 便宜 end up near each other in the latent space, because they were fitted against the same blanks. The prediction gets thrown away with W′. The arrangement is what you keep.

Two consequences worth carrying into the rest of this chapter.

What word2vec gives youWhat it cannot give you
Relations between individual tokens, averaged over the whole corpus — the initial understanding of meaning, nothing more. One vector per token, so every sense shares it. 词典的一个词会有多个意思; the entry is the union, and the sentence is not consulted.
Objective meaning: the statistics of what people actually wrote, independent of any one author's intent. Subjective meaning: that appears only when an author composes these words in this order — a property of the sentence, not of the dictionary.

The right-hand column is the job description for everything that follows. word2vec compiles the dictionary; self-attention reads the sentence — it is the layer that takes those author-independent vectors and lets a particular context bend them.

What context does to a dictionary entry

Here is that handoff made concrete. 美女 is in the dictionary with one objective entry: a beautiful woman. Now put it in two sentences:

the sentencewhat 美女 now means
美女 — on its ownthe dictionary entry, unmodified: good-looking
美女，加一下微信
“Miss, let's swap WeChat”		the entry, more or less intact — the speaker probably does mean it
美女，麻烦让一下
“Miss, excuse me, coming through”		the entry, largely drained — it has become a form of address and says nothing about looks

Nothing changed about the token. What changed is the company it is keeping. So:

A sentence's meaning is the dictionary's meanings, expanded and edited — and the edit is hidden in the context. That is the job. Attention's specific task is to work out how much, and in which direction, each surrounding token revises each other token's objective entry.

Read the attention formula with that sentence in hand and it stops being arbitrary:

termwhat it is
Vthe objective meaning, as looked up — the dictionary entry word2vec compiled, one row per token
softmax(QKᵀ/√Dout)the edit coefficients — how strongly this context revises each entry
the productthe entry after this particular sentence has had its say

Which leaves exactly one question, and it is the one the rest of this page answers: why should QKᵀ produce the right coefficients? Nothing so far says it must.
